key_terms.meaning: At equilibrium p_A = H x_A, or for dilute systems y_A = m x_A, linking gas partial pressure to liquid concentration.
Pressure per unit liquid mole fraction; m = H/P is the dimensionless equilibrium slope.
Plot of solute-free gas ratio Y = mol solute/mol carrier gas against liquid ratio X = mol solute/mol solvent.
Locus of Y* in equilibrium with X; for dilute absorption Y* = mX.
Solute balance between any point and one end of the absorber; for dilute counter-current absorption Y = (L/G)X + constant.
Vertical gap Y − Y* at a given X, or X* − X at a given Y.
Smallest L/G that can reach the specified Y_out; the operating line touches the equilibrium line.
Point where operating and equilibrium lines touch at minimum solvent; driving force is zero.
Gas and liquid flow in the same direction; operating line moves toward equilibrium and driving force falls along the column.
Gas and liquid flow in opposite directions; operating line stays farther from equilibrium, giving larger average driving force.
Gas contacts fresh liquid in successive stages; several operating lines or a stepped path, not one straight line.
A = L/(mG), ratio of operating-line slope to equilibrium-line slope; A > 1 gives finite stage count.
Analytical relation between N, A and solute recovery for straight equilibrium and operating lines.
Wetted interfacial area per unit volume of packed bed, m²/m³.
Fraction of packed-bed volume that is empty, dimensionless.
Empirical packing characteristic used in pressure-drop and capacity correlations.
Height of an overall gas-phase transfer unit, m; includes gas and liquid film resistances.
Number of overall gas-phase transfer units, dimensionless; set by equilibrium and operating lines.
Absorption in which heat of solution changes liquid temperature and hence solubility.
E = actual absorption rate with reaction ÷ physical absorption rate without reaction.
Transfer of one or more gas components into a liquid solvent.
Removal of dissolved gas from a liquid by contact with a gas lean in that solute.
Moles of solute per mole of carrier gas or solvent, excluding the solute itself.
An ideal contact stage in which outgoing gas and liquid are in equilibrium.
Ratio of actual solute removed on a tray to solute removed by an ideal theoretical stage.
Height equivalent to a theoretical plate; packed height needed per equilibrium stage, m.
K_G a combines overall gas-phase coefficient K_G and interfacial area per volume a, kmol/(m³ s Δy).
Absorption in which the dissolved solute reacts chemically with the solvent or a reagent in it.

takeaways: Solubility fixes equilibrium, and Henry's law turns dilute gas-liquid equilibrium into a straight line on a Y–X plot.
The operating line is a solute balance; the vertical gap between it and the equilibrium line is the driving force.
The minimum liquid-to-gas ratio occurs when the operating line touches the equilibrium line at a pinch.
Counter-current contact gives more average driving force than co-current contact and is the usual choice for absorption.
The absorption factor A = L/(mG) measures how far the liquid rate exceeds the minimum and controls the number of stages.
Packing area a, void fraction ε and packing factor Fp decide interfacial area, capacity and pressure drop.
Packed height Z = H_OG × N_OG separates the mass-transfer coefficient from the separation duty.
Heat release raises liquid temperature and lowers solubility; reaction consumes solute and raises the rate through E.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine equilibrium and operating lines, minimum solvent, stage or NTU–HTU design, and a comment on thermal or reactive effects.

bank.q: State Henry's law in the form p_A = H x_A and explain how it becomes Y* = mX on a solute-free plot.
outline: define p_A, x_A and H
convert dilute y = m x to Y ≈ y and X ≈ x
straight equilibrium line through the origin for dilute absorption
effect of temperature on H and m

bank.q: Compare co-current, counter-current and cross-current gas-liquid contact for absorption. Include operating-line shape and average driving force.
outline: co-current: same direction, operating line ends at equilibrium, low driving force
counter-current: opposite directions, largest average driving force, standard absorber
cross-current: gas contacts fresh liquid in stages, no single straight operating line
choice depends on recovery, solvent rate and pressure drop

bank.q: Define absorption factor A = L/(mG). Explain how its value controls the number of theoretical stages.
outline: L and G are solute-free liquid and gas rates
m is the equilibrium-line slope
A > 1 gives finite stages; A near 1 needs many stages
Kremser equation links A, N and recovery

bank.q: Define specific surface a, void fraction ε and packing factor Fp for a tower packing. State one design use of each.
outline: a is wetted area per packed volume
ε is empty volume fraction
Fp is an empirical pressure-drop characteristic
a gives interfacial area; ε gives holdup and capacity; Fp gives pressure drop

bank.q: Explain why non-isothermal absorption can reduce or destroy the driving force in a packed absorber.
outline: heat of solution raises liquid temperature
solubility falls as temperature rises
equilibrium line moves up or becomes curved
driving force shrinks; a temperature bulge may appear

bank.q: A gas has Y_in = 0.05 and Y_out = 0.005. Equilibrium is Y* = 25X. Fresh solvent has X_0 = 0. Calculate the minimum L/G.
outline: X* at inlet gas = Y_in/m = 0.002
operating line at minimum passes through (X*, Y_in)
L/G_min = (Y_in − Y_out)/(X* − X_0)
answer 22.5

bank.q: For the same gas, use L/G = 1.5 times the minimum and find the outlet liquid mole ratio X_1.
outline: solute balance: L(X_1 − X_0) = G(Y_in − Y_out)
X_1 = (Y_in − Y_out)/(L/G)

bank.q: A tray absorber has A = 1.4 and N = 6 theoretical stages. Use the Kremser equation to estimate the fraction of solute removed when Y_in = 0.04, X_0 = 0 and m = 2.
outline: Kremser absorption equation for A ≠ 1
compute Y_out from N, A and mX_0
fraction removed = (Y_in − Y_out)/Y_in
state assumptions: straight equilibrium and operating lines

bank.q: A packed absorber has H_OG = 0.8 m and N_OG = 5.5. Find Z. State why H_OG and N_OG are separated in design.
outline: Z = H_OG N_OG
H_OG contains mass-transfer coefficient and flow rates
N_OG contains equilibrium and operating lines

bank.q: A packed tower must handle a foaming, corrosive gas with a high liquid rate. Choose between random packing, structured packing and trays, and justify using a, ε and Fp.
outline: random packing: cheap, good for corrosive service, lower capacity
structured packing: high area, low pressure drop, poor for fouling
trays: good for high liquid, fouling and heat removal
use a, ε and Fp to compare area, capacity and pressure drop

bank.q: Compare tray and packed absorbers for recovery, pressure drop, turndown and maintenance. Recommend one for a service with corrosive solvent and frequent cleaning.
outline: tray: discrete stages, easy cleaning, higher pressure drop
packed: low pressure drop, high area, but cleaning difficult
corrosive service favours plastic or ceramic packing or trays
frequent cleaning favours trays or large-pitch packing
recommendation with reasons

bank.q: Analyse the effect of exothermic absorption on column design. Explain when an isothermal design is unsafe and how a non-isothermal design changes the operating and equilibrium lines.
outline: heat of solution raises liquid temperature
m rises with temperature so the equilibrium line steepens
operating line changes if liquid rate or temperature changes
driving force falls, so more height or area is needed
isothermal design is unsafe for high heat of solution and concentrated solute

bank.q: Evaluate multicomponent absorption with a reacting solvent. Explain why one equilibrium line is not enough, how solutes compete, and what the enhancement factor changes.
outline: each solute has its own m and equilibrium line
write a solute balance for each component with a common solvent
competition for solvent lowers driving force for some components
reaction consumes solute and raises rate
E = rate with reaction ÷ physical rate
E depends on kinetics, concentration and contact time

bank.q: Evaluate the idea of operating an absorber at the minimum liquid-to-gas ratio. Include pinch, column height and solvent pumping cost.
outline: at minimum L/G the operating line touches equilibrium at the pinch
driving force is zero at the pinch so height becomes infinite
operate above minimum, commonly 1.2 to 2 times
more liquid lowers stage height but raises pumping and regeneration cost
optimum balances capital and operating cost

glossary.def: Transfer of one or more gas components into a liquid solvent.
Removal of dissolved gas from a liquid by contact with a gas lean in that solute.
Moles of solute per mole of carrier gas or solvent, excluding the solute itself.
At equilibrium the partial pressure of a gas equals a constant times its liquid mole fraction.
The locus of gas compositions in equilibrium with liquid compositions at a fixed temperature and pressure.
The locus of gas and liquid compositions that satisfy the solute balance in a contactor.
The difference between actual composition and equilibrium composition at a point in the contactor.
A point where the operating line meets the equilibrium line, making the driving force zero.
The smallest solvent flow per gas flow that can achieve a specified separation.
An ideal contact stage in which outgoing gas and liquid are in equilibrium.
Ratio of actual solute removed on a tray to solute removed by an ideal theoretical stage.
A = L/(mG), comparing the liquid flow capacity with the equilibrium slope.
A formula relating the number of stages, absorption factor and solute recovery for straight lines.
Interfacial area per unit volume of packed bed, usually m²/m³.
The fraction of the packed-bed volume that is empty space.
An empirical number for a packing used to estimate pressure drop and capacity.
Height equivalent to a theoretical plate, the packed height per equilibrium stage.

glossary.term: Height of an overall gas-phase transfer unit
glossary.def: H_OG, the packed height that gives one overall gas-phase transfer unit.

glossary.term: Number of overall gas-phase transfer units
glossary.def: N_OG, the dimensionless separation duty obtained from equilibrium and operating lines.
K_G a, the overall gas-phase coefficient multiplied by interfacial area per unit volume.
Absorption in which heat release changes the liquid temperature and therefore the solubility.
E = actual absorption rate with reaction ÷ physical absorption rate without reaction.
Absorption in which the dissolved solute reacts chemically with the solvent or a reagent in it.
Absorption of two or more solutes into one solvent, where each solute has its own equilibrium line.
